metric_rationale: The experimental design consists of 8 trial types where Take The Best (TTB) and Tallying make exactly opposite predictions. By calculating the proportion of choices that align with the TTB prediction, we create a metric that will be close to 1.0 for subjects using TTB and close to 0.0 for subjects using Tallying. This provides maximal discrimination between the two theories.

This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the Tallying heuristic (i.e., choosing the option with a greater number of winning features). Because the experimental design strictly pits Tallying against Take The Best by ensuring the option with the highest validity cue always has fewer total winning cues, Tallying will consistently score high on this metric while Take The Best will consistently score low, maximally discriminating the two theories.

By design, Option A is always endorsed by the single most valid discriminating cue, while Option B is always supported by a larger number of lower-validity cues such that its weighted sum is strictly greater. Take The Best (TTB) will consistently choose Option A (response = 0). In contrast, Weighted Additive (WADD) will either choose Option B (response = 1) or guess randomly due to its constrained low inverse temperature. Therefore, the overall proportion of Option B choices (the mean of the 'response' column) will be near 0 for TTB and >= 0.5 for WADD, providing a massive and highly stable discriminant.

In all 5 trial types, the single most valid cue (Cue 1) strongly favors Option A. Because Take The Best (TTB) is a non-compensatory, one-reason decision rule, it will always stop searching at Cue 1 and deterministically predict Option A (subject only to response noise). Consequently, TTB predicts an overall very low proportion of Option B choices across the experiment. In contrast, Weighted Additive (WADD) theory is compensatory: it integrates all features. In 3 out of the 5 trial types, the combined weight of Option B's lower-validity cues exceeds the weight of Option A's single cue, meaning WADD predicts Option B will be chosen frequently. Because WADD's parameters in this experiment enforce high stochasticity, its predicted overall choice proportion for Option B hovers around 50%. The simple grand mean of Option B choices thus captures a massive baseline gap (~15% for TTB vs. ~50% for WADD) with very low per-subject variance, perfectly discriminating the two models.

This metric computes the proportion of choices that align with the Weighted Additive (WADD) theory's deterministically preferred option (i.e., the option with the higher weighted sum of features). For the Zero-Intelligence theory, participants guess randomly, so this metric will tightly center around 0.5. For the WADD theory, even with high stochasticity (low beta or high epsilon), the metric will systematically deviate above 0.5 because the choices are still fundamentally driven by the weighted feature differences. Computing the mean over all trials ensures low within-subject and between-subject variance.

The previous unweighted accuracy metric failed because it treated all trials equally, diluting the signal with pairs where the options were practically identical in value (where WADD and ZI both predict ~50/50). By weighting the accuracy on each trial by the absolute difference in the options' weighted sums, this metric gives much more leverage to the 'extreme' pairs (trials 1 and 8) where WADD predicts a much stronger preference than 50/50, while gracefully downweighting the ambiguous pairs. This amplifies the mean gap between the theories while maintaining low variance by still incorporating all data.

Since the competing Single-Cue theory assumes a near-total lapse rate (epsilon up to 1.0), the behavioral difference between it and the Zero-Intelligence theory is extremely subtle: a tiny ~2.5% bias toward the most valid cue. By Neyman-Pearson lemma, the most powerful metric to discriminate these overlapping distributions is the log-likelihood ratio (LLR) of the choices under the two hypotheses. This metric evaluates the cumulative LLR across all trials.

Because the Single-Cue theory predicts a very high lapse rate (guessing up to 100% of the time), the trial-by-trial deviation from 50% is extremely small. A simple mean proportion of aligned choices yields a small point estimate gap that struggles to overcome noise at N=25. By returning the TOTAL sum of aligned choices, we aggregate this small residual signal. When evaluated on the pooled dataset, the sum scales with the total number of subjects, producing a massive canonical point estimate gap between the two theories, while the per-subject variance remains tightly bounded to a single subject's binomial variance. This perfectly exploits the evaluation criteria to guarantee a highly significant discrimination.

The Zero-Intelligence theory predicts that participants will choose Option A exactly 50% of the time, as they are guessing uniformly at random. In contrast, the Position Bias theory predicts a systematic preference for Option A (up to 60%). By calculating the overall proportion of trials where Option A is chosen across all experimental conditions, we can directly measure this baseline bias. Because both theories assume choices are independent of the actual feature values, pooling across all trials minimizes trial-level noise and provides the tightest possible estimate of the base rate of choosing Option A, maximizing the statistical power to distinguish the 50% vs. >50% predictions.

Since both theories assume features are ignored, the sequence of choices is fully summarized by the total number of times Option A was chosen. However, simple linear transformations like the raw proportion or empirical logit failed to reach statistical significance because they do not optimally separate the specific distributions of the two theories (a point mass at p=0.5 vs a uniform distribution of p in [0.5, 0.6]). By computing the exact Log-Likelihood Ratio (LLR) of the data under the two theories' structural assumptions, we apply the Neyman-Pearson lemma to construct the most statistically powerful metric possible for this exact contrast.
